senses: To expose to great heat.
To be exposed to great heat.
ety: From Middle English broylen, brulen (“to broil, cook”), from Anglo-Norman bruiller, broiller (“to broil, roast”), Old French brusler, bruller (“to broil, roast, char”), a blend of two Old French verbs: * bruir (“to burn”), from Frankish *brōjan (“to burn, scald”) * usler (“to scorch”), from Latin ustulō (“to scorch”)

senses: the point whose (Cartesian) coordinates are the arithmetic mean of the coordinates of a given finite set of points.
ety: From centre + -oid. From 1844, used as a replacement for the older terms "centre of gravity" and "centre of mass" in situations described in purely geometrical terms, and subsequently used for further generalisations.

senses: A feeling or state of being demotivated.
To walk; go about.
To traffic in an itinerant manner; to peddle.
To turn; play a trick.
ety: From Middle English tranten, from or cognate with Middle Dutch tranten (“to step, walk”), perhaps ultimately from Proto-Germanic *trent-, *trant- (“to walk”). Cognate with West Frisian trantsje (“to step, step time; dance, jump”). Compare also Dutch drentelen (“to saunter”).

senses: Of food: elaborate and complex, like that prepared by an expert chef.
Resembling, involving, or being cider.
examples: The more he heard of fumbled passes, cidery kisses and snapped straps, the more he knew better than to risk such humiliation.

senses: A person with amnesia.
A medication with amnesic effects.
Somewhat new
One who, or that which, conserves.
Any of several insects, usually shield-shaped, possessing a gland that produces a foul-smelling liquid, usually containing aldehydes, which they use to discourage predators.
An area of land, marked for studying its plants, animals, soil, natural processes, etc.
ety: Borrowed from Latin quadrātum. Doublet of quadrate and of etymology 2 below.

senses: Somewhat gold in colour.
ety: From Middle English goldissh, equivalent to gold + -ish.

senses: To make or become salty or salted
A convertible (automobile); its convertible top.
examples: Johnny imagines all manner of chrome gadgetry that he could kipe and give to his father to jazz up his ’fifty-six Ford Vicky ragtop.

senses: The degree to which a reaction is regioselective.
The state or quality of being solid.
Moral firmness; validity; truth; certainty.
ety: From solid + -ity, from Middle French solidité, from Latin soliditās.

senses: A roadside restaurant in South Asia.
Any restaurant that serves Punjabi food.
A person who intentionally causes the destruction of property in order to hinder the efforts of their enemy.
source; findspot; origin
provenance, history
ety: Borrowed from Latin prōveniēns, present participle of prōvenīre (“to come up”); compare provene, provenient, and provenance.

senses: Extremely angry; wrathful; enraged.
ety: From Latin īrātus (“angered, angry”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from īrāscor (“to be angry”), from īra (“anger, wrath”).

senses: A racquet sport popular in Spain and Latin America, usually played in doubles on a small, closed court.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish pádel, from English paddle (tennis).

senses: A view of an area of the Moon.
A desolate or devastated landscape.
examples: In the Australian outback, industrial activity — notably open-pit coal mining — has turned verdant areas into moonscapes seemingly overnight, and the suicide rate in the region has skyrocketed.
They made their way to a geological formation called Kap Kobenhavn, a series of bare hills as desolate as a moonscape.

They had never managed to host many events on their property, in part because some of the surrounding area remained a moonscape. The cork oak where Phillip wanted his ashes spread had burned down in the last fire.

senses: A person who adheres to the philosophy of consequentialism.
The insertion of the buds of one plant into another; grafting.
An inoculum; that which is inoculated.
Synonym of prebunking.
Any technique to reduce harm by exposing oneself to a milder form of that harm.
ety: From Latin inoculātio. Equivalent to inoculate + -ion.

senses: The system or practice of a cult.
Synonym of culteranismo.
ety: From cult + -ism. The linguistic sense is from Spanish cultismo.
examples: Also keep in mind that the Democrats of today are part of a new woke cultism – They are not necessarily the same Democrats from 30 years ago.

senses: Magnetic friction in dynamos, by which every reversal of magnetism in the iron causes dissipation of energy.
ety: Coined by Sir James Alfred Ewing from Ancient Greek ὑστέρησις (hustérēsis, “shortcoming”), from ὑστερέω (husteréō, “I am late, fall short”), from ὕστερος (hústeros, “later”). By surface analysis, hyster- (“higher, outer, latter, next”) + -esis.

senses: The act or process of racializing, that is, of treating (a relationship, practice, person or group) in racial terms or of constituting (that person or group) as racial or as a race.
In Ancient Egypt, a heavy beaded necklace and musical instrument with a crescent-shaped plate in the front and a keyhole-shaped amuletic counterweight in the rear, considered sacred to Hathor.
The keyhole-shaped counterweight of such a necklace, considered an amulet to secure divine protection and to ensure fertility.
ety: Borrowed from Egyptian mnjt in the form of the 19th-century Lepsius-style transcription menȧt.

senses: The state of being damned; condemnation; openly expressed disapprobation.
ety: From Middle English dampnacioun, from Old French dampnacion, from Latin damnatio.

senses: A jester dressed entirely in red.
A tapered steel mandrel used by a jeweler to make jewelry.
ety: From French triboulet, an eponym from the jester Triboulet (1479 – 1536) of kings Louis XII and Francis I of France.

senses: An Ancient Greek pitch-marking diacritic: ⟨ ` ⟩; written atop vowels, it denotes normal or low pitch.
A theory or belief that the whole is greater than the sum of the parts.
A practice based on such a theory or belief.
ety: From hol- (“whole, entire, total”) + -ism. Coined in 1926 by Jan Smuts.

senses: Cheap, inferior; pretentious.
Words collectively, considered in a mass sense.

examples: But the plates are good, and, in reality, sufficient without all the wordage.

senses: A military man; a soldier.
ety: From French militaire. Doublet of military.

one who cuts hair; a barber
one who registers voters or conducts a poll

ety: Borrowed from Spanish milagro (“miracle”), from Latin mīrāculum. Doublet of miracle and miraculum.

senses: Between the vertebrae
An illation.
ety: From Late Latin illātīvus (“illative”), from Latin illātus, perfect passive participle of inferō (“carry or bring into somewhere; bury; conclude”), from in + ferō (“bear, carry; suffer”).
